title: 13 — Security Engineering
html:
13 — Security Engineering

Framing: security is not a feature you add; it's a property of decisions made throughout the system. Your job as a senior engineer is to know which decisions have security consequences and to make them the safe way by default.

1. Core principles

Principle Meaning Practical application
Defence in depth Multiple independent layers; assume any one fails WAF and input validation and parameterised queries and least-privilege DB user
Least privilege Every identity gets the minimum access needed App DB login is not db_owner; service principals scoped per resource; short-lived tokens
Fail secure On error, deny An exception in an authorisation check must deny, never allow
Complete mediation Check authorisation on every access, server-side Hiding a button is UI polish, not security
Zero trust Never trust the network position Authenticate and authorise service-to-service calls too
Secure by default The safe option requires no configuration HTTPS on, cookies Secure+HttpOnly, deny-by-default CORS
Minimise attack surface Fewer endpoints, dependencies, ports, features Delete unused endpoints and packages
Don't roll your own crypto Really Use platform primitives and vetted libraries
Assume breach Design so a breach is detectable and contained Segmentation, audit logs, encryption at rest, short credential lifetimes

The CIA triad: Confidentiality (only the right people see it), Integrity (it hasn't been tampered with), Availability (it's there when needed). Every control maps to one; every trade-off is usually one against another.

2. Threat modelling

Do it once per significant feature, in ~45 minutes, with the team.

Four questions (Shostack):

  1. What are we building? (a data-flow diagram)
  2. What can go wrong? (STRIDE)
  3. What are we going to do about it?
  4. Did we do a good job?

STRIDE:

Threat Property violated Example Control
Spoofing Authentication Forged JWT, stolen session Strong authN, MFA, signature verification
Tampering Integrity Modified request body, poisoned cache Signatures, HTTPS, server-side validation
Repudiation Non-repudiation "I never approved that trade" Immutable audit log with identity and time
Information disclosure Confidentiality IDOR, verbose errors, PII in logs AuthZ, encryption, generic errors
Denial of service Availability Resource exhaustion, ReDoS, zip bomb Rate limits, quotas, timeouts, size limits
Elevation of privilege Authorisation Mass assignment of IsAdmin, path traversal AuthZ checks, explicit binding, sandboxing

Trust boundaries are where the model earns its keep: anywhere data crosses from a less-trusted zone to a more-trusted one (browser→API, API→DB, service→third party, user upload→processor). Validate at every boundary.

3. OWASP Top 10 — with the .NET/Angular specifics

A01 — Broken Access Control (the #1 real-world cause of breaches)

IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference):

// ❌ Any authenticated user can read any portfolio by changing the id
[HttpGet("portfolios/{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Get(int id, CancellationToken ct)
    => Ok(await _repo.GetAsync(id, ct));

// ✔ Authorisation is part of the query, not a separate check that can be forgotten
[HttpGet("portfolios/{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Get(int id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var userId = User.GetUserId();
    var portfolio = await _repo.GetForUserAsync(id, userId, ct);   // scoped by owner
    return portfolio is null ? NotFound() : Ok(portfolio);          // 404, not 403 — don't leak existence
}

Rules: deny by default ([Authorize] globally via a fallback policy, [AllowAnonymous] on the exceptions); check authorisation server-side on every request; scope every query by tenant/owner; never trust an ID, role, or tenant from the client.

// Global deny-by-default
builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .SetFallbackPolicy(new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder().RequireAuthenticatedUser().Build());

Resource-based authorisation for anything beyond role checks:

var authResult = await _authorization.AuthorizeAsync(User, portfolio, Operations.Update);
if (!authResult.Succeeded) return Forbid();

A02 — Cryptographic Failures

Requirement Do Don't
Passwords Argon2id (preferred) or bcrypt/PBKDF2 with high iterations; ASP.NET Identity's default hasher is fine MD5, SHA-256 alone (fast = brute-forceable), custom "salt + hash" schemes
Data in transit TLS 1.2+ everywhere, HSTS, no mixed content Plain HTTP anywhere, disabled cert validation
Data at rest TDE/disk encryption + column encryption for the most sensitive fields Storing PAN/secrets in plaintext
Random values RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes() / crypto.getRandomValues() Random, Guid.NewGuid() for tokens, Math.random()
Symmetric encryption AES-GCM (authenticated) AES-CBC without a MAC (padding-oracle attacks)
Comparison of secrets CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals == on tokens/HMACs (timing attack)
Key management Key Vault / KMS, rotation, separate keys per environment Keys in config, code, or the same store as the data 
// Secure token generation
public static string NewSecureToken(int bytes = 32) =>
    Base64UrlTextEncoder.Encode(RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(bytes));

// Constant-time comparison for API keys / HMACs
bool valid = CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(
    Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(providedKey), Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(expectedKey));

Hash vs encrypt vs encode — get this right:

  • Encoding (Base64, URL-encoding) is not security. It's a format.
  • Hashing is one-way. For passwords, use a slow, salted, memory-hard hash.
  • Encryption is two-way and requires key management, which is the hard part.
  • Signing/HMAC proves integrity and origin, not confidentiality.

A03 — Injection

SQL injection:

// ❌ Concatenation — the vulnerability, regardless of how "safe" the input looks
var sql = $"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'";

// ✔ Parameterised (Dapper)
const string Sql = "SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE email = @Email";
var user = await conn.QuerySingleOrDefaultAsync<User>(Sql, new { Email = email });

// ✔ EF Core: LINQ parameterises automatically; FromSqlInterpolated is also safe
var users = await db.Users.FromSqlInterpolated(
    $"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = {email}").ToListAsync(ct);   // interpolation → parameter
// ⚠️ FromSqlRaw($"...{email}...") is NOT safe — the string is built before EF sees it

⚠️ Dynamic SQL for sorting/filtering is the common leak even in parameterised codebases: ORDER BY {column} can't be parameterised. Validate against an allow-list:

private static readonly FrozenSet<string> SortableColumns =
    new[] { "trade_date", "notional", "instrument_code" }.ToFrozenSet();

if (!SortableColumns.Contains(sortBy))
    throw new ArgumentException($"Invalid sort column '{sortBy}'.", nameof(sortBy));

Other injections: OS command (Process.Start with user input — avoid shell invocation, pass args as an array), LDAP, XPath, NoSQL ({ $where: userInput } in Mongo — never), template injection, and log injection (a newline in user input forging log entries — sanitise or use structured logging).

A04 — Insecure Design

Threat model. Prefer secure patterns: idempotency keys, rate limits, immutable audit, deny-by-default. You cannot patch your way out of a design that requires the client to be trustworthy.

A05 — Security Misconfiguration

  • Debug/detailed errors off in production (app.UseExceptionHandler, not UseDeveloperExceptionPage).
  • Default credentials changed; sample apps and Swagger UI removed or protected in prod.
  • Directory listing off; unnecessary HTTP methods disabled.
  • Security headers:
app.Use(async (ctx, next) =>
{
    var h = ctx.Response.Headers;
    h["X-Content-Type-Options"]  = "nosniff";
    h["X-Frame-Options"]         = "DENY";                       // or CSP frame-ancestors
    h["Referrer-Policy"]         = "strict-origin-when-cross-origin";
    h["Permissions-Policy"]      = "geolocation=(), camera=(), microphone=()";
    h["Content-Security-Policy"] =
        "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-" + nonce + "'; " +
        "style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self' https://api.example.com; " +
        "frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'";
    await next();
});
app.UseHsts();   // Strict-Transport-Security — production only, and understand it's sticky

⚠️ CSP is the highest-value header and the hardest to adopt. 'unsafe-inline' in script-src defeats most of its XSS protection — use nonces or hashes. Roll it out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first and watch the reports.

A06 — Vulnerable and Outdated Components

dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive
npm audit --omit=dev

Automate: Dependabot/Renovate for updates, SCA scanning in CI with a policy (fail on Critical/High), an SBOM for anything you ship, and lockfiles committed. Transitive dependencies are the majority of your attack surface.

A07 — Identification and Authentication Failures

  • MFA for anything privileged.
  • Rate-limit and lock out on failed logins (with care — account lockout is a DoS vector; prefer exponential delay + CAPTCHA + anomaly detection).
  • Generic error messages: "Invalid email or password", never "no such user" (username enumeration).
  • Rotate the session ID on login and on privilege change (session fixation).
  • Secure password reset: single-use, short-lived, high-entropy token; don't reveal whether the email exists; invalidate all sessions on password change.
  • Check credentials against a breached-password list (Have I Been Pwned k-anonymity API).
  • No arbitrary complexity/rotation rules — NIST guidance is length ≥ 8 (encourage passphrases), block known-breached passwords, and don't force periodic rotation.

A08 — Software and Data Integrity Failures

Insecure deserialisation:

// ❌ BinaryFormatter is removed in .NET 9 for exactly this reason — RCE by design
// ❌ Newtonsoft with TypeNameHandling.All/Auto on untrusted input = RCE
var settings = new JsonSerializerSettings { TypeNameHandling = TypeNameHandling.All };  // NEVER on user input

// ✔ System.Text.Json with explicit types, no polymorphic type resolution from the payload
var dto = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<CreateOrderRequest>(json, JsonOpts.Strict);

Mass assignment / over-posting:

// ❌ Binding straight to the entity: a crafted payload can set IsAdmin, Balance, TenantId
public async Task<IActionResult> Update(User user) { ... }

// ✔ A DTO with exactly the fields the client may set
public sealed record UpdateProfileRequest(string DisplayName, string? Bio, string? TimeZone);

Supply chain: pin dependency versions, verify signatures, use trusted registries, review what your CI has access to (a compromised action can exfiltrate every secret), and sign your artifacts.

A09 — Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

Log: authentication successes and failures, authorisation denials, privilege changes, password/MFA changes, data exports, admin actions, and input-validation failures at the boundary. Include: who, what, when, from where, and the correlation ID. Never log: passwords, tokens, session IDs, full card numbers, API keys, or full request bodies containing PII.

// ❌ log.LogInformation("Login attempt {@Request}", request);   // request contains the password
// ✔
log.LogInformation("Login attempt for {EmailHash} from {ClientIp} — {Outcome}",
    Hash(request.Email), clientIp, outcome);

Alert on: spikes in 401/403, impossible-travel logins, mass data export, new admin grants, and disabled logging.

A10 — Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

// ❌ Fetching a user-supplied URL — the classic cloud-credential theft
var content = await _http.GetStringAsync(userSuppliedUrl);
// attacker supplies http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance → cloud IAM credentials

Controls: allow-list of destination hosts; resolve the DNS name and reject private/link-local/loopback IP ranges (and re-check after redirects — DNS rebinding); disable redirects; use a dedicated egress proxy with no metadata access; and prefer IMDSv2-style metadata protections.

4. Web-specific attacks

4.1 XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)

Type Where the payload lives
Stored Persisted in the database, served to every viewer (worst)
Reflected In the URL/query, echoed back
DOM-based Never reaches the server; client-side JS writes untrusted data into the DOM

Angular's protections: interpolation {{ value }} is auto-escaped; [innerHTML] is sanitised by DomSanitizer. ⚠️ bypassSecurityTrustHtml disables that — every use needs a justification comment and a review.

// ❌ Never with user-controlled input
this.html = this.sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(userContent);

// ✔ Bind text; if you must render HTML, sanitise with DOMPurify and an allow-list
this.safeHtml = DOMPurify.sanitize(userContent, { ALLOWED_TAGS: ['b','i','em','strong','a','p','ul','li'] });

Server side: encode on output, contextually (HTML body vs attribute vs JS vs URL vs CSS — different encodings). Razor @value encodes; @Html.Raw does not. CSP with nonces is the backstop for whatever you miss.

4.2 CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)

Only relevant when the browser attaches credentials automatically — i.e. cookie-based auth. A Authorization: Bearer header sent by JS is not auto-attached, so token-in-header APIs are not CSRF-vulnerable (but are then exposed to XSS token theft — see §4.4).

Defences (use at least two):

  1. SameSite=Lax (default) or Strict on the auth cookie — blocks most cross-site sends.
  2. Anti-forgery token (synchroniser token or double-submit cookie). ASP.NET Core: [ValidateAntiForgeryToken], or for SPAs the XSRF-TOKEN cookie + X-XSRF-TOKEN header pattern (Angular's HttpClient does this automatically with HttpClientXsrfModule).
  3. Verify Origin/Referer on state-changing requests.

4.3 Clickjacking

X-Frame-Options: DENY or CSP frame-ancestors 'none'. Required for anything with authenticated actions.

4.4 Where to store a token in a browser

Storage XSS risk CSRF risk Verdict
localStorage Any XSS steals it None Common, but the token is exfiltratable
sessionStorage Same None Same problem, shorter life
JS-readable cookie Same Yes Worst of both
HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie JS cannot read it Yes → add anti-forgery Recommended
In-memory only (+ refresh via HttpOnly cookie) Lost on reload; smaller window None for the access token Best security, more plumbing

Recommendation for an Angular + ASP.NET Core app: HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Lax cookie for the session, plus anti-forgery tokens on state-changing requests. It removes the "XSS = permanent account takeover" outcome.

5. Authentication & authorisation

5.1 The vocabulary

  • Authentication (authN) — who are you? → 401 when it fails.
  • Authorisation (authZ) — what may you do? → 403 when it fails.
  • Identity provider (IdP) — issues tokens (Entra ID, Auth0, Keycloak, Okta).
  • OAuth 2.0 — a delegated authorisation framework. It is not an authentication protocol.
  • OpenID Connect (OIDC) — an authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0. It adds the ID token. Use OIDC for login; use OAuth for API access. Conflating them is the most common misunderstanding.

5.2 OIDC Authorization Code flow with PKCE (the only flow you should use for apps)

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as App (SPA or server)
    participant I as Identity provider
    participant R as Resource API
    A->>A: generate code_verifier;<br/>code_challenge = S256(verifier)
    A->>I: /authorize?response_type=code&code_challenge=...&state=...&nonce=...
    I->>U: login + consent
    U->>I: credentials + MFA
    I->>A: redirect with ?code=...&state=...
    A->>A: verify state matches
    A->>I: POST /token {code, code_verifier, client_id}
    I->>A: id_token (who), access_token (what), refresh_token
    A->>R: GET /resource  Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
    R->>R: validate signature (JWKS), iss, aud, exp, nbf, scope
    R->>A: 200

Why PKCE: it binds the authorization code to the client that started the flow, so an intercepted code is useless. Mandatory for public clients (SPA, mobile) and now recommended for all clients. state prevents CSRF on the callback; nonce binds the ID token to this authentication request (replay protection). ⚠️ Never use the implicit flow or the resource-owner-password flow in new code. Both are deprecated.

5.3 JWT — what to actually verify

header.payload.signature   (base64url, dot-separated)
{"alg":"RS256","kid":"abc"} . {"sub":"u1","iss":"...","aud":"api","exp":...,"scope":"read:portfolios"} . <sig>

options.TokenValidationParameters = new TokenValidationParameters
{
    ValidateIssuer           = true,  ValidIssuer   = cfg["Auth:Issuer"],
    ValidateAudience         = true,  ValidAudience = cfg["Auth:Audience"],
    ValidateLifetime         = true,  ClockSkew     = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),  // default 5 min is generous
    ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true,
    ValidAlgorithms          = ["RS256"]           // pin the algorithm
};

⚠️ JWT pitfalls:

  • alg: none and algorithm confusion (RS256 token verified as HS256 using the public key as the HMAC secret) — pin ValidAlgorithms.
  • A JWT cannot be revoked before expiry. Keep access tokens short (5–15 min) and use refresh tokens with rotation and reuse detection. For instant revocation you need a check against a denylist or a reference token — which reintroduces state, and that's a legitimate trade-off to state out loud.
  • Don't put PII or secrets in the payload — it's base64, not encrypted, and readable by anyone holding it.
  • Don't use a JWT as a session cookie without understanding you've traded revocability for statelessness.

5.4 Authorisation models

Model Rule Use
RBAC Permissions attach to roles; users get roles Simple, coarse-grained. Most apps start here
ABAC Policy over attributes of user, resource, action, environment "Managers can approve trades under £1M in their own desk during market hours"
ReBAC Permissions derive from relationships in a graph Sharing/hierarchies (Google Zanzibar, OpenFGA)
Policy engines Externalised rules (OPA/Rego, Cedar) Many services sharing one policy

⚠️ Don't put permissions in roles claims and forget them. A token issued before a permission change carries stale authority for its lifetime. For sensitive operations, check authority at the time of the action, from the source of truth.

// Policy-based authorisation in ASP.NET Core: express the rule, not the role
builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("CanApproveTrade", p => p.Requirements.Add(new TradeApprovalRequirement()));

public sealed class TradeApprovalHandler(TimeProvider clock)
    : AuthorizationHandler<TradeApprovalRequirement, Trade>
{
    protected override Task HandleRequirementAsync(
        AuthorizationHandlerContext ctx, TradeApprovalRequirement req, Trade trade)
    {
        var isOwnDesk  = ctx.User.FindFirst("desk")?.Value == trade.Desk;
        var underLimit = trade.Notional <= req.MaxNotional;
        var isApprover = ctx.User.IsInRole("TradeApprover");
        // Four-eyes: an approver cannot approve their own trade
        var notSelf    = ctx.User.GetUserId() != trade.CreatedBy;

        if (isApprover && isOwnDesk && underLimit && notSelf) ctx.Succeed(req);
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

5.5 Service-to-service

Managed identity / workload identity federation (no secret at all) > client credentials with a rotated secret > API key. Add mTLS inside a mesh. Propagate the end-user identity as a signed token (on-behalf-of flow) rather than dropping to a service identity — otherwise you lose per-user authorisation in downstream services.

6. Input validation & output encoding

Validate at the boundary, in this order:

  1. Syntactic — type, length, format, range. Reject early.
  2. Semantic — does it make sense in the domain? (a date not in the future, an ID that exists and belongs to the caller)
  3. Allow-list over deny-list. Enumerate what's permitted; blocklists are always incomplete.
  4. Canonicalise before validating (URL-decode, Unicode normalise) or the check can be bypassed by encoding.
public sealed class CreateTradeValidator : AbstractValidator<CreateTradeRequest>
{
    public CreateTradeValidator()
    {
        RuleFor(x => x.InstrumentCode).NotEmpty().Length(1, 12).Matches("^[A-Z0-9.]+$");
        RuleFor(x => x.Notional).GreaterThan(0).LessThanOrEqualTo(1_000_000_000m);
        RuleFor(x => x.TradeDate).LessThanOrEqualTo(_ => DateOnly.FromDateTime(DateTime.UtcNow));
        RuleFor(x => x.Currency).Must(BeSupportedCurrency).WithMessage("Unsupported currency.");
    }
}

File uploads — a checklist, because every item here has caused a real breach:

  • Size limit enforced at the proxy and the app
  • Extension and content-type and magic-byte sniffing all checked against an allow-list
  • Generate a new random filename; never use the client's (path traversal: ../../web.config)
  • Store outside the web root, ideally in object storage
  • Serve with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
  • Never execute; never place in a directory with execute permissions
  • Virus scan for anything user-shared
  • Guard against zip bombs and XML entity expansion (billion laughs) — cap decompressed size and disable DTD processing

ReDoS: a catastrophic-backtracking regex like ^(a+)+$ on a 40-character input hangs a CPU core. Set RegexOptions.NonBacktracking (.NET 7+) or a matchTimeout, and never build a regex from user input.

7. Secrets management

Rule Detail
No secrets in source control Enforce with gitleaks/trufflehog in CI and a pre-commit hook
No secrets in images or logs Inject at runtime; scrub log output
Prefer no secret at all Managed identity / workload identity federation
Vault everything else Key Vault / Secrets Manager, access-audited
Rotate Scheduled, automated, and support two valid values during rotation
Scope per environment Dev secrets must be useless in prod
On leak: rotate first Then scrub history. The credential is compromised the moment it's pushed; a force-push doesn't un-clone it 
// Managed identity — no secret to leak, no rotation to manage
builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(
    new Uri($"https://{vaultName}.vault.azure.net/"), new DefaultAzureCredential());

8. Secure SDLC

flowchart LR
    D[Design<br/>threat model, ADR] --> C[Code<br/>secure defaults, review]
    C --> B[Build<br/>SAST, secret scan, SCA, SBOM]
    B --> T[Test<br/>DAST, authZ tests, fuzzing]
    T --> R[Release<br/>signed artifacts, least-privilege deploy]
    R --> O[Operate<br/>WAF, monitoring, patching, IR]
    O -.lessons.-> D
Stage Tooling
SAST CodeQL, SonarQube, Roslyn analyzers, dotnet format --verify
Secret scanning gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning, pre-commit hooks
SCA Dependabot/Renovate, dotnet list package --vulnerable, npm audit, Snyk
Container Trivy, Grype, Defender for Containers
DAST OWASP ZAP, Burp
IaC Checkov, tfsec, Bicep linter
Runtime WAF, Defender, Falco, anomaly alerts

Policy: fail the build on Critical/High with a documented, time-boxed exception process. A scanner whose findings are always ignored is worse than no scanner — it manufactures false assurance.

9. Privacy & compliance (the engineering parts)

Requirement Engineering implication
Data minimisation Don't collect what you don't need; the safest PII is the PII you never stored
Purpose limitation Don't reuse data for a new purpose without a lawful basis
Right to erasure You need a tested delete path across primary store, replicas, backups, caches, search index, logs, and analytics. ⚠️ Design this on day one — retrofitting it into an event-sourced or heavily-replicated system is brutal (crypto-shredding is the usual escape hatch)
Right to access/portability An export path per data subject
Retention Automatic deletion after the retention period, per data class
Data residency Region-pinned storage and processing; watch third-party subprocessors
Breach notification 72 hours under GDPR — you need detection and an incident process to meet it
PCI DSS Don't store PAN. Use a tokenising provider and keep your systems out of scope
Audit Immutable, tamper-evident logs of access to sensitive data

Practical: classify every field (Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted-PII) in the schema documentation, and let the classification drive encryption, logging, masking, and retention rules automatically.

10. Incident response

  1. Detect — alerting on the signals in A09.
  2. Triage — is it real? What's the blast radius? Declare severity.
  3. Contain — revoke credentials, disable the account/endpoint, block the IP, isolate the host. Preserve evidence before you rebuild.
  4. Eradicate — patch, rotate every credential that could have been exposed, rebuild from known-good.
  5. Recover — restore service, monitor closely for re-entry.
  6. Learn — blameless postmortem, notify per legal obligation, track remediations to completion.

Pre-agree: who can declare an incident, who can take production down, who talks to legal/customers, and where the runbook lives. Deciding this during the incident costs hours.

11. Checklist & interview angles

Pre-release security checklist

  • Threat model done for new trust boundaries
  • AuthN required by default; [AllowAnonymous] audited
  • AuthZ checked server-side for every resource access, scoped by tenant/owner
  • All queries parameterised; dynamic SQL identifiers allow-listed
  • Input validated at the boundary; output contextually encoded
  • Secrets from a vault; nothing in code, config, images, or logs
  • TLS everywhere; HSTS; certificates monitored
  • Security headers incl. a CSP without unsafe-inline
  • Rate limiting and payload size limits on public endpoints
  • Dependencies scanned; no known Critical/High
  • Security events logged with correlation; no secrets or PII in logs
  • Errors generic to the client, detailed in logs
  • File uploads: type, size, name, storage, and serving all handled
  • Data classified; retention and deletion paths implemented and tested
  • Least-privilege identities for app, CI, and infrastructure

🔍 Interview angles

  • Authentication vs authorisation? Who you are (401) vs what you may do (403); both must be server-side, and authorisation must be checked on every access, not just at navigation time.
  • How do you prevent SQL injection? Parameterised queries always; allow-list any identifier that can't be parameterised. Not escaping, not a WAF.
  • Where should a SPA store its JWT? Preferably nowhere JS can read — an HttpOnly cookie plus anti-forgery tokens. localStorage means any XSS is full account takeover.
  • OAuth vs OIDC? OAuth is delegated authorisation (access tokens for APIs); OIDC adds authentication and the ID token. Use Authorization Code + PKCE.
  • How do you revoke a JWT? You can't, cleanly — short lifetimes plus refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, or a denylist/reference tokens if instant revocation is required.
  • What is CSRF and when does it not apply? Forged state-changing requests using ambient credentials; not applicable when credentials are sent explicitly by JS in a header rather than automatically by the browser.
  • You find a secret committed to git. What now? Rotate it immediately, then assess exposure, then clean history. Rotation first, always.
  • How would you secure an internal service-to-service call? Workload identity + mTLS + per-service authorisation, propagating the end-user identity — never "it's on the internal network so it's fine".
